summary.text: 次 is used for “next,” “in sequence,” and “second in rank.” Manuscripts from the Qin and Han periods attest ordered and ranked uses, while interpretations of the earliest graph remain disputed.

formation.text: The earliest construction is disputed. One interpretation of an oracle-bone form proposes a military-station sign; other accounts describe a person exhaling or a speaking figure with possible saliva marks. The later Shuowen analysis treats 次 as 欠 plus 二, with 二 as a sound element, but does not settle the origin of the earlier forms.

components.text: In the Shuowen analysis, 欠 is the pictorial element: it evokes a person with an open mouth or exhaling. Other interpretations also describe an exhaling or speaking figure, but this does not establish 欠 as a component of the earliest graph.
Shuowen assigns 二 a phonetic role in 次. The reported Old Chinese comparison shows similar endings, but does not independently confirm that 二 supplied the sound.

sound_limitation.text: The reported reconstruction comparison does not independently establish that 二 is the phonetic component in 次.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, 二 and 次 have a comparable final sequence. This is the sound comparison behind the proposal, but it does not establish 二 as 次’s phonetic component.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze examples are recorded, followed by Qin-slip, seal, clerical, and regular-script forms. One interpretation of an oracle-bone form combines an element identified as an early form of 師 with two strokes indicating an encampment, proposing a military-station sign. Other interpretations differ, and this proposed scene remains uncertain.

Some bronze forms are described with marks below 欠 or short strokes. Whether this reflects regularization, corruption, or a meaningful graphic change is unresolved. Shuowen later analyzes 次 as 欠 plus 二 and assigns 二 a sound role; that analysis remains disputed.

uncertainties.text: Interpretations of the earliest graph differ: proposals include a military-station sign, a person exhaling, and a speaking figure with possible saliva marks. The military-station proposal concerns an oracle-bone form; the available descriptions do not resolve these readings.
Shuowen’s analysis of 二 as a sound element is historically important, but the reported reconstruction comparison does not independently confirm that role.

No securely dated semantic path connects a proposed early meaning to “next” or “in sequence.” The lodging and tent examples come from transmitted texts whose witnesses are not dated in the cited accounts.

senses.gloss: in sequence; next or second in rank
senses.text: Qin- and Han-period manuscript citations attest 次 for ordered transmission and successive rank. These uses are established by that period, but do not show that they were the graph’s original meaning.
Transmitted texts use 次 for lodging or tents. How these uses relate to ranked and ordered meanings is unresolved.

A Han silk manuscript is reported to use 次 to write 恣. This proposed borrowing reuses 次 for another word on the basis of sound resemblance, rather than a change in 次’s meaning; the cited account gives no pronunciations to demonstrate the match.

A Mawangdui manuscript is reported to use 次 where the transmitted Zhouyi has 濟. This proposed borrowing reuses 次 for another word on the basis of sound resemblance, rather than a change in 次’s meaning; the cited account gives no pronunciations to demonstrate the match.

limitations.text: The Qin- and Han-period attestations do not establish the first occurrence of ordered or ranked uses, or their derivation from any proposed original sense. No semantic link is asserted where the evidence does not demonstrate one.
次 is reported in place of 恣 and 濟 in separate manuscripts, but the cited material gives no pronunciations to demonstrate or independently assess the proposed sound-based borrowings.

overview.text: 次 means “next,” “in order,” or “second in rank.” Qin- and Han-period manuscripts attest ordered and ranked uses; interpretations of the earliest graph differ.

components.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictures an open-mouthed or exhaling person; this does not settle the earliest graph’s form.
Shuowen treats 二 as a sound element. A reported sound comparison motivates this proposal, but does not prove 二 supplied 次’s sound.

relationships.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictorially represents an open-mouthed or exhaling person within 次.
Shuowen analyzes 二 as the phonetic element in 次; this role remains disputed.
